bull.b: Baker Hughes has moved from losses in 2021–2022 to solid profitability, while operating and free cash flow remain strong. This improves earnings quality, supports investment across growth markets, and provides internally generated funds for debt reduction and shareholder returns.

Record IET remaining performance obligations and book-to-bill above one provide meaningful revenue visibility beyond the current quarter. The backlog supports forward planning, reinforces customer demand for Baker Hughes equipment and services, and reduces reliance on immediate order activity.

Chart expands Baker Hughes beyond traditional oilfield exposure into cryogenic equipment, LNG infrastructure, data-center power and other industrial applications. This broader portfolio can improve resilience across energy cycles while creating cross-selling opportunities and a larger aftermarket base.

bear.b: The acquisition-related increase in leverage raises interest expense and reduces financial flexibility even as operating results improve. Debt reduction is now a capital-allocation priority, which may constrain discretionary investment, acquisitions or shareholder distributions until balance-sheet strength recovers.

A growing mix of long-cycle projects strengthens future backlog but delays conversion into reported revenue and cash generation. This can produce uneven growth, increase dependence on project execution, and limit the near-term benefit of strong bookings despite healthy underlying demand.

bear.t: Execution, inflation and regional operating pressure
bear.b: Regional disruption, logistics constraints and inflation can raise delivery costs and pressure project margins across IET and OFSE. If these pressures persist, they could delay execution, reduce cash conversion and offset some of the profitability gains expected from stronger orders and portfolio expansion.
